function_question: How does nature store energy to jump?

opening.text: There was a girl called Leila who lived above a tiny toy shop full of spinning tops, puppets and wind-up cars.
After school, Leila pressed her nose to the shop window and dreamed up toys of her own.
The owner sighed. "Kids want a toy that jumps, but every jumping toy needs batteries. Leila, can you invent one that doesn't?"

card.hero: Leila, a toy inventor in training
card.place: A toy shop that needs a new toy
card.problem: The shop wants a toy that jumps without batteries

guide.brief: I'm Popi, your story guide. Leila's toy shop needs a toy that jumps with no batteries at all. Can you help her? Let's start!
guide.your_idea: Some inventors already have a springy idea bouncing around. Do you?
guide.nature_clues: Nature's jumpers were storing energy long before rubber bands existed. Tap each card to meet four champion jumpers!
guide.design_secret: Here's the secret all four heroes share…
guide.skill: Scientists predict before they test. Which rubber band will make the card pop the highest? Point it away from faces.
guide.sketch: Time to draw your toy loaded and ready, like a real toy designer!
guide.build_and_test: Build your grasshopper, load it, lock it and let it go. How many centimetres high can it jump?
guide.retry_tip: Inventors never stop at round 1. Change just ONE thing, like the band or the catch, and jump again!
guide.ending: And ever since then, Leila's grasshopper is the shop's best-selling toy, and it has never needed a single battery.

quick_check.question: A flea is 2 mm long and can jump 100 times its own length. How far is that?
quick_check.right: Right! 2 mm × 100 = 200 mm, and 200 mm is 20 cm. That's about the length of a pencil!
quick_check.wrong: Not quite. Work out 2 mm × 100 first, then remember that 10 mm is 1 cm.

clue_cards.name: Flea
clue_cards.trick: A pad of super-springy resilin, held squashed by a catch.
clue_cards.does: When the catch lets go, the pad snaps and flings it over 100 times its length.

clue_cards.name: Kangaroo
clue_cards.trick: Long, stretchy tendons in its back legs.
clue_cards.does: They store energy on every landing and spring back to power the next hop.

clue_cards.name: Click beetle
clue_cards.trick: A peg that locks its bent body like a trigger.
clue_cards.does: When the peg slips, the body snaps straight and flips it into the air.

clue_cards.name: Frog
clue_cards.trick: Very long back legs folded up tight.
clue_cards.does: The legs unfold into long levers that fling it far forward.

match_groups.label: 🔒 A catch that locks, then snaps
📏 Long legs that act like levers

predict.prompt: Stores energy or not? Predict first!

items.label: A ball of clay squashed flat

predict.explain: Springy things store energy when you bend, squash or stretch them, and give it back when you let go. Clay just stays squashed, so its energy is lost.

lab.title: The pop-up card lab
lab.predict: Fold each jumping card flat and let go. Which band will make it pop the highest?

tool.name: How Might We
tool.intro: You already know U (the user) and N (their need). Today you'll learn the last 2 pieces: I for Insight and H for the How Might We question itself.

parts.name: Insight
parts.what: Something surprising you noticed about the user.
parts.example: 🎒 Kids hang their bag on one shoulder because it's quicker to grab.
parts.starter: I noticed that kids in the toy shop love toys that…

parts.name: How might we…?
parts.what: Mix user, need and insight into one hopeful question.
parts.example: 🎒 How might we make a bag that's quick to grab AND kind to backs?
parts.starter: How might we make a toy that jumps high without…
